title: Comparative 2 (much better / any better etc.)
subtitle: much better / any better / better and better
summary: Learn how to make a comparative stronger or weaker with much, a bit, any and no, and how to use better and better and the ... the ... .

lesson.heading: much / a lot + comparative
lesson.text: You can put these words before a comparative to say how big the difference is: **a bit**, **a little**, **slightly** (= a little), **much**, **a lot**, **far** (= a lot).

examples.text: I felt ill earlier, but I feel **much better** now.
Don't go by train. It's **a lot more expensive**.
Could you speak **a bit more slowly**?
This bag is **slightly heavier** than the other one.
The problem is **far more serious** than we thought at first.

lesson.heading: any / no + comparative
lesson.text: You can also use **any** and **no** before a comparative (any longer, no bigger etc.). They mean 'not even a little'. Use **any** with a negative verb or in a question; use **no** with a positive verb.

examples.text: I've waited long enough. I'm not waiting **any longer**.
We expected their apartment to be very big, but it's **no bigger** than ours.
examples.note: or ... it isn't any bigger than ours

examples.text: How do you feel now? Do you feel **any better**?
This hotel is better than the other one, and it's **no more expensive**.

lesson.heading: better and better
lesson.text: We repeat a comparative (better and better, more and more expensive etc.) to say that something changes continuously.

examples.text: Your English is improving. It's getting **better and better**.
The city has grown fast in recent years. It's got **bigger and bigger**.
As I listened to his story, I became **more and more convinced** that he was lying.
**More and more tourists** are visiting this part of the country.

lesson.heading: the sooner the better
lesson.text: You can say **the sooner the better**, **the more the better** etc. to mean 'as soon as possible', 'as much as possible'.

examples.text: *A:* What time shall we leave? *B:* **The sooner the better.**
*A:* What sort of bag do you want? A big one? *B:* Yes, **the bigger the better.**
When you're travelling, **the less** luggage you have **the better**.

lesson.heading: the ... the ... (one thing depends on another)
lesson.text: We also use **the ... the ...** with two comparatives to say that one thing depends on another thing.

examples.text: **The sooner** we leave, **the earlier** we'll arrive.
examples.note: = if we leave sooner, we'll arrive earlier

examples.text: **The younger** you are, **the easier** it is to learn.
**The more expensive** the hotel, **the better** the service.
**The more** I thought about the plan, **the less** I liked it.

lesson.heading: older and elder
lesson.text: The comparative of *old* is **older**. We use **elder** only about people in a family (my elder sister, their elder son), and *older* is possible there too. We never say that somebody 'is elder'.

examples.text: David looks **older** than he really is.
My **elder** sister is a TV producer.
My sister is **older** than me.

lesson.text: Remember: *any* and *no* come before comparatives too - use *any* after a negative or in a question (I'm not waiting any longer), and *no* after a positive verb (it's no bigger than ours).

exercises.prompt: This bag is too small. I need something ___.
exercises.explanation: much + comparative shows a big difference: much bigger.

exercises.prompt: It was very hot yesterday. Today it's ___.
exercises.explanation: a little + comparative shows a small difference: a little cooler.

exercises.prompt: I liked the museum. It was ___ I expected.
exercises.explanation: a lot + comparative + than: a lot more interesting than I expected.

exercises.prompt: You're driving too fast. Can you drive ___?
exercises.explanation: slowly is a long word, so the comparative is more slowly: a bit more slowly.

exercises.prompt: I'm afraid the problem is ___ it seems.
exercises.explanation: far means 'a lot', and than introduces what we compare with.

exercises.prompt: I've waited long enough. I'm not waiting ___.
exercises.explanation: any + comparative after a negative verb: not even a little longer.

exercises.prompt: The traffic isn't especially bad today. It's ___ usual.
exercises.explanation: The verb is positive (It's), so we use no + comparative + than. We would need a negative for any: It isn't any worse than usual.

exercises.prompt: That hole in your sweater is getting ___.
exercises.explanation: A repeated comparative shows a continuous change: bigger and bigger.

exercises.prompt: Since Anna went to Canada, her English has got ___.
exercises.explanation: The irregular comparative of good is better, repeated: better and better.

exercises.prompt: Match the two halves of these the ... the ... sentences.

pairs.right: the easier it is to learn.
the higher your bill will be.
the harder it is to concentrate.

exercises.prompt: We should decide what to do as soon as possible. Put the parts in the right order.
exercises.answer: The sooner we decide what to do, the better.
exercises.explanation: the sooner ... the better = as soon as possible.

exercises.statement: I'm surprised Anna is only 25. I thought she was elder.
exercises.explanation: I thought she was older. We never say that somebody 'is elder' - elder only goes before a family word, as in my elder sister.
